meta.title: Who really said "Every election is a sort of advance auction sale of stolen goods"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — H. L. Mencken wrote it, in his essay “Sham Battle,” Baltimore Evening Sun, 26 October 1936. The Ambrose Bierce credit is a later error.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every election is a sort of advance auction sale of stolen goods'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Mencken: “Sham Battle,” Baltimore Evening Sun, 26 October 1936. Later re-credited to Ambrose Bierce as an “advanced auction” — both wrong.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Mencken wrote it in an essay called “Sham Battle” in The Evening Sun of Baltimore on 26 October 1936, in the sentence “government is a broker in pillage, and every election is a sort of advance auction sale of stolen goods.” The essay was later reprinted in the 1956 collection A Carnival of Buncombe. Unusually for a line pinned on Mencken, the popular short form is not a paraphrase — it is his own clause, lifted intact.

source.excerpt: In other words, government is a broker in pillage, and every election is a sort of advance auction sale of stolen goods.
trail: 26 October 1936 — the origin. Quote Investigator's study of the saying identifies the source as Mencken's essay “Sham Battle,” published in the Baltimore Evening Sun on 26 October 1936, and concludes that Mencken can properly be credited with the statement in his 1936 essay ↗. No citation earlier than that essay appears anywhere in QI's article.

The 1956 collection. QI notes the essay was reprinted in A Carnival of Buncombe, edited by Malcolm Moos; the Internet Archive's catalogue record confirms the volume as H. L. Mencken, A Carnival of Buncombe, Johns Hopkins Press, Baltimore, 1956, 370 pages ↗. Its contents include a section headed “Roosevelt & Alf” — the 1936 campaign.

Wikiquote agrees on the author, not on the wording. Wikiquote carries the passage in its 1940s–present section for Mencken with the clause transposed to “every election is sort of an advance auction sale of stolen goods,” cited not to the 1936 column but to Charting the Candidates ’72 (1972) by Ronald Van Doren, p. 7 ↗. The 1936 wording QI transcribes reads “a sort of.”

No rival claimant survives. The competing credit is to Ambrose Bierce. Quote Investigator states plainly that it found no substantive evidence that Ambrose Bierce said or wrote this comment ↗, and dates the Bierce credit no earlier than 2006.
source.cutTag: The closing sentence of the passage
source.excerptNote: Mencken builds to it rather than opening with it. The argument running ahead of this sentence, paraphrased: the state is a gang of men no better than anyone else, whose only real talent is getting and holding office; they win it by finding groups who want something they cannot have and promising to supply it; nine times in ten the promise is worthless, and the tenth time it is honoured by looting one group to pay another. Quote Investigator transcribes the full passage ↗.

source.rightsNote: The line comes from a newspaper essay first published on 26 October 1936 and reprinted in a 1956 book — both well after the 1931 cut-off, so this text is treated as in copyright in the United States, not public domain. author.name: H. L. Mencken
author.heading: The Sage of Baltimore
author.metaLine: 1880–1956 · American journalist, satirist and cultural critic
author.bio: Henry Louis Mencken was born in Baltimore on 12 September 1880 and spent essentially his whole career there, joining the city's newspapers in 1899 and writing for The Sun, The Evening Sun and The Sunday Sun until a stroke ended his writing life in 1948. He co-founded The American Mercury in 1924, produced the landmark study The American Language, and made his name nationally with his savage coverage of the 1925 Scopes trial — the “Monkey Trial,” a phrase he popularised. A lifelong sceptic of mass democracy, he opposed the New Deal at real cost to his popularity, and the compressed, contemptuous style of that opposition is exactly why so many unsourced cynicisms get pinned on him — and why this one, for once, turns out to be real.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Mencken is one of the internet's great fake-quote magnets, so the surprise here is that the line is genuinely his. What travels wrongly is the wording — and, since the mid-2000s, the name attached to it.

items.why: By 2006 the saying was being credited to Bierce; Quote Investigator quotes a collection of essays and poetry, Beyond Bougie by Stephen Earley Jordan II, introducing it as Bierce speaking “in his cynical, yet honest ways.” QI reports finding no substantive evidence that Bierce said or wrote it ↗. The pull is obvious — Bierce wrote The Devil’s Dictionary, and the line reads like one of its entries — but the earliest documented instance is Mencken's, in 1936.

items.who: “nothing more than an advanced auction of stolen goods”
items.why: The most-circulated variant is not Mencken's phrasing. QI records Robert J. Ringer's 2000 book giving it as “an election is nothing more than an advanced auction of stolen goods” — advance hardened into advanced, sale dropped, and nothing more than was added. QI tracks that drift ↗, and it is this altered form that the 2006 Bierce credit carries.

items.who: “every election is sort of an advance auction sale”
items.why: A transposed order circulates widely and is what Wikiquote prints, citing Charting the Candidates ’72 (1972) by Ronald Van Doren, p. 7 ↗ rather than the 1936 column. QI's transcription of the essay reads “a sort of advance auction sale.”

misattribution.truthLine: The short form quoted everywhere — “every election is a sort of advance auction sale of stolen goods” — is word-for-word Mencken's own clause, and Quote Investigator credits him with it in the 1936 essay ↗. It is the “advanced auction” version, and the Bierce byline, that are counterfeit.

context.heading: Written eight days before a landslide
lead: The essay ran in Baltimore on 26 October 1936. The presidential election was held on 3 November 1936 — eight days later — and it went overwhelmingly against everything Mencken was arguing: Franklin D. Roosevelt took 60.8% of the popular vote and 46 of the 48 states, burying Alf Landon and consolidating the New Deal coalition.

That is the joke buried inside the line. Mencken was writing at the peak of his opposition to the New Deal, in a campaign fought squarely over whether the federal government should spend to relieve hardship. Where Roosevelt saw relief, Mencken saw a transaction: politicians locating groups who want what they cannot have, promising it, and paying for it out of somebody else's pocket. His verdict on that machinery — government as a broker in pillage — is what makes the auction metaphor bite rather than merely sneer.
context.detailsSummary: Where the essay ended up, and why the line hides in a newspaper
detailsBody: Twenty years on, the essay was gathered into A Carnival of Buncombe (Johns Hopkins Press, 1956), the collection of Mencken's political journalism edited by Malcolm Moos and published the year he died. Its contents run through the campaigns he covered — “Normalcy,” “Onward Christian Soldiers: Hoover & Al,” “Roosevelt Minor,” “Roosevelt & Alf.”

Mencken had been at the Baltimore papers since 1899 and kept writing for The Sun, The Evening Sun and The Sunday Sun until a stroke stopped him in 1948. The 1936 essay sits inside that long newspaper run, which is why the sentence never turns up in the books people reach for — and why it took a dedicated search of the column archive to place it.
